speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext: On May 5th an order of the house was passed for the production of papers regarding the prosecution of Harry Bronfman. The papers that were brought down refer only to the Department of National Revenue and the evidence on which the investigating commission, found a prima facie case against Harry Bronfman. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) informed the house that the other papers were confidential and could not be furnished. Will the Minister of Justice now furnish those papers, or will he say why the crown was not in a position to make out a good case at law, to use his own words in answer to the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine)?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext: As the hon. gentleman says, the return was prepared by the Department of National Revenue, and apparently they tabled everything except the legal opinions sent to that department by the Deputy Minister of Justice. Those legal opinions, under the practice that has always prevailed, are as a matter of fact private documents and are never made public. My hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) tells me that another hon. member, I think the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), asked for the same papers, and the minister communicated them to him personally and he was satisfied. Perhaps my hon. friend from Rose-town will be satisfied if the Minister of National Revenue shows him the report of the Deputy Minister of Justice.

subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext: I do not think that that would satisfy me because it is only the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, and the Minister of Justice has already given his decision in the matter. What we want to know is why the crown was not in a position to make out a good case at law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext: That will be indicated in the opinion.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext:
The question which the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) has asked is not in form just what I proposed to ask the minister, having read in Hansard the reply he gave the other day, namely, that the crown in right of the Dominion had concluded that there was not sufficient evidence on which to predicate a prosecution being taken against a certain person.
[Mr. Robb.l
My understanding is that that is a matter that must rest with the provincial authorities. Time and time again the Dominion government has declined to exercise the power because it can exercise it only through the attorney general's department in the respective provinces. For instance, the crown in right of the Dominion, cannot prosecute a case in the provinces. The crown can assist by having somebody act with the attorney general of the province, but it is perfectly obvious that the crown in right of the Dominion cannot carry on the prosecution. I could not help overhearing a remark on the other side as to the Saskatchewan election, but this has nothing whatever to do with the Saskatchewan election. In connection with prosecutions under the Combines Act in regard to the fruit industry, counsel for the Dominion came into the provinces, and the only method by which the prosecution was carried on was by the indictment being preferred through the department of the attorney general of the province. Counsel for the Dominion assisted or acted on behalf of the provincial authorities in carrying forward the prosecution. It has never been competent, in my judgment, for this Dominion or for the Minister of Justice to determine whether or not proceedings should be taken against anybody. That rests with the provincial authorities, because the administration of justice rests with them only, and all the power in this parliament could not enter a nolle prosequi against an individual in connection with criminal proceedings. That must come from the attorney general of the province If my memory serves me-I intended to look it up, but as my hon. friend from Rosetown has brought the question up, I may now state my recollection-Sir John Thompson considered this point very carefully at one time in connection with certain prosecutions that arose out of the McGreevy-Connolly difficulties, and the conclusions that were arrived at then were approved by such eminent jurists as the Hon. David Mills and Mr. afterwards, Sir Louis Davies. I am speaking wholly from memory and subject to correction, but my memory is that the principle is there emphatically laid down that there is no power in the Dominion to declare that a prosecution shall or shall not be taken against any alleged offender against the law, but that power rests in the attorney general of the province, the provincial authorities alone being the power charged with the administration of criminal justice. Even although the Minister of Justice thought that the case in question was not a good case for criminal prosecution and so

Penny Bank Act
advised the Department of National Revenue, the duty of the department is to transmit the documents to the attorneys general in the respective provinces affected, and have the appropriate attorneys general take such proceedings as may be necessary, first determining either not to prosecute or to proceed with the case. I dare say that my friend the Minister of Justice and certainly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will remember that the former member for South York (Mr. Maclean), always urged that there should be power in this parliament under our constitution, as there is in the United States, for the federal prosecuting officers and federal marshals to prosecute and carry on proceedings in the several courts for the purpose of enforcing justice. We have not that power under our constitution. He used to point out with a great wealth of learning that the effect of that lack of power was to render the enforcement of many of our federal statutes ineffective and inefficient, and he suggested from time to time that our constitution should be so amended as to provide beyond perad-venture that this Dominion could itself institute and carry forward criminal proceedings. Certainly the federal government has no power to enter a nolle prosequi and no officer of our Dominion, the Solicitor General or the Minister of Justice, can discontinue criminal proceedings or, in the sense in which the word is properly used, initiate or continue them in the criminal courts of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext:
I quite agree with my
lion, friend that there is no power on the part of this government to file a nolle prosequi, but there is power to refrain from laying a charge-

subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext: Oh yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext:
That is exactly what
has been done in this case. The officers of the Department of Justice, after having received the evidence taken before the royal commission, came to the conclusion that in law we had not a good case against Bronfman, and the Department of National Revenue was so advised.
As far as the attorney general of the province is concerned I quite agree, too, that all indictments must be proffered toy the attorney general, but surely there must be somebody to initiate something. Especially when it comes from the federal authorities, the attorney general of the province never acts unless some federal officer lays a complaint against somebody, and then it becomes the duty of the attorney general to prosecute. But when the federal authorities come to
the conclusion that they cannot prosecute and do not lay any complaint or charge against the man before the provincial authorities, I do not think the provincial authorities can be blamed for not prosecuting.

subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext:
Then am I to understand
that the whole responsibility rests on the Justice department at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext:
Responsibility only so
far as I have indicated. When a legal opinion is asked of the Department of Justice by any of the departments of the government, certainly we are responsible for the answer, but that is all.

subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext: The value of that opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice is only this, that it expresses the view of a responsible minister of the crown, a federal minister, that such a prosecution would not succeed, but it cannot in any sense stay or bind or limit or restrict the duty of the attorney general of the province to enforce the laws of the country if charges are brought before the court for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext:
If charges are brought.
May I add that any citizen of Canada can lay a complaint if anybody is not satisfied. If my hon. friend from Rosetown is not satisfied, he can lay a complaint himself.

subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN
speechtext: Did not the commission itself lay a charge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: '1 CUSTOMS AND EXCISE PROSECUTIONS -MR. HARRY BRONFMAN

On Section 1, subsection 2-Withdrawals for investment on other approved securities.
What is the general purpose of this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Penny banks are purely philanthropic in purpose. The Penny Bank of Ontario serves a school population of 170,000 children in 360 schools in 85 municipalities throughout the country, all the chartered banks acting as local agents of the Penny Bank. Under the charter as they have it now, Mr. Chairman, they may invest their funds only in Dominion of Canada securities. This bill is to widen their powers so that they may invest in Dominion of Canada
Penny Bank Act

guaranteed securities, or securities of, or guaranteed by, any province of Canada, or of the government of the United Kingdom, or of any municipal corporation in Canada, including debentures issued for public school purposes or guaranteed by any such municipal corporation, as the minister may approve. The board may also invest, to an amount not exceeding 50 per cent of the funds at the credit of the bank as aforesaid, in first mortgages on improved real estate in the Dominion of Canada not exceeding 50 per cent of the value thereof.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance how this bank differs from any other bank; how is it able to use the word " bank " which is more or less of a monopoly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have just given my hon.
friend and the house the information as to their loaning privileges. Heretofore, they have only been able to invest money in Dominion government securities. Many of those securities will mature shortly. They desire now to widen their powers so that they may invest in guaranteed securities of the Dominion of Canada, in guaranteed securities of the provinces, or of the United Kingdom, or any of the municipalities, and an amount not to exceed 50 per cent may be invested in first mortgages on improved real estate in the Dominion of Canada subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance. It is purely a philanthropic organization. There are no shareholders and the directors receive no fees.

I only put it to the minister, if he does not think it desirable to eliminate that for the reason that it suggests a moral obligation on the part of the minister to become responsible for the validity and sufficiency of those loans, and I do not think that is quite sound.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 254, respecting the construction by the Canadian National Railway Company of certain terminal facilities with grade separation and other works at and in the vicinity of the city of Montreal.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I would like that to stand if
possible. There is certain information I desire and I propose to make some observations in connection with this bill when I get that information. We should think very carefully about certain matters connected with the bill, and I propose possibly to offer an amendment in the way of a section to be added. As this bill was before the committee for a few hours the other day, and involves an enormous sum of money, I think we should proceed carefully with it.

I have no objection to
letting it stand, but perhaps it would facilitate matters if my hon. friend would mention the points touching which he wishes information. If he does so I shall be glad, if possible, to supply that information.

Very well, we can go into committee.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 2-Power to construct and build works described in the schedule.

The minister will recall
that by statute we validated an agreement made between the Canadian Northern Terminal Company and the Canadian Northern Railway Company, whereby this country became obligated, as conditions now are, to pay a certain annual sum in interest and sinking fund with respect to securities involved in the construction of the old Canadian Northern terminal. I have not had an opportunity to investigate the matter, but I was in the house when it went through and I took occasion then to go into the question with a good deal of care. That is why I suggest that it would be well for us to look into the matter thoroughly; personally I should like to find out, first of all, what annual charge there is now against Canada in connection with the construction of the old terminal-that is, the tunnel terminal. It involves the payment of a fixed sum for a certain number of years by way of rental, being equivalent to interest and sinking fund on securities issued for the purpose of constructing the terminal. Of course, I am speaking now only from memory; I have not had a chance to verify the facts. The other day I attended a meeting of the railway committee and I may observe that I can find no record of the proceedings. I thought that minutes of that meeting were being taken, but so far as I can find out, there was no shorthand report of it. Is that correct?

I do not know of any,
no.

Two or three observations were then made which in my judgment should be carefully considered. One was that at the end of ten years the property would pay 6 per cent on investments. Some of the members of the committee thought that meant the whole terminal investment; obviously all that was meant was as respects the passenger station. I spoke to one of the directors of the system afterwards and he told me that this interpretation which I placed upon the matter was correct. There are no buildings contemplated by this bill apart from terminal buildings as such, and any buildings which would yield revenue, such as comes from the New York Central properties like the Bilt-more hotel, for example, would have to be provided for by private capital or from the resources of the public. Whit respect to this matter I should like to have some more definite idea. I listened also to the estimates that were given as to cost of construction, but they were so vague and general that I decided to ask the minister-not being a member of the committee I could not discuss the matter there-whether he would be able to give us a more detailed idea of just what was involved.
Lastly, it apparently is contemplated that we should continue the Bonaventure station. A high level construction from that station would carry the rails into St. Henri to connect with the inner belt line, if I may use that term; because the system contemplates two belt lines, an outer and an inner, which of course is something in the nature of the scheme that now prevails in England with respect to the Metropolitan-an inner and an outer belt line. At one time the old Bonaventure street station was to be abandoned; that is how I understood the plans, as I could gather them.
It still is, as a station.

But it is not being abandoned, in this sense, that it is now being utilized under the new scheme, and there will be an enormous expenditure in connection with carrying the rails at high level from that station through St. Henri. That was the impression I formed, listening the other day to the explanation. Is it correct?

My hon. friend is under
some misapprehension which I shall clear up.

At any rate that was
what I gathered. I gathered further that this was because of the recommendations made by Mr. Palmer. My understanding was that the first plans prepared by the Canadian National engineers did not contemplate that, but that the recommendations of Mr. Palmer contem-

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
plated the connecting up of the tunnel lines with the Bonaventure street station, by means of high level rails from Bonaventure to St. Henri, thereby making that a circle of the inner belt line-the inner circle, as they call it in England. I could not hear very well all that was said, but that was what I gathered would be the effect of the proposal. I could hear the answers given to some questions asked by the hon. member for St. Henri (Mr. Mercier), but I could not catch the questions themselves. Perhaps the minister would give us some information in this regard.
Some observations were made also with respect to other reports which, I understood, had been made by engineers employed by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I suggest that these reports be made available to hon. members who may wish to consult them. I could not gather what the names of the engineers were, but I thought one was Smith. I made inquiries of one of the Canadian Pacific Railway representatives and he informed me that such a report had been made, but I have not seen it, and I fancy that possibly the minister will let us have access to it.
I wish to be frank with the minister. Apparently the state of public opinion in this country is pretty much what it was prior to 1914; we are willing to spend money regardless of w'here it comes from or where it may lead us to. Twenty-one years ago this fall I ventured to express rather a strong opinion with respect to railway expenditures in Canada, and I am bound to say that I received 1'ittie support at that time; but ten years later everyone said I had been right. Now I am not suggesting that I am right in this instance inasmuch as I have not arrived at any definite conclusion, but I do desire to point out to the committee-at least I shall do so on the third reading oh the bill-where I think this leads to, and how serious it is that we should involve ourselves in the expenditure of such enormous amounts without having before us more detailed information as to the causes that necessitate these expenditures. As I have said, I speak now only what occurs to me at the moment, but both the province of Saskatchewan and the province of Alberta were called upon, under guarantee in connection with the old roads, to pay money, and the guarantees in those cases amounted to only $13,000 a mile.
Fifteen thousand.

Fifteen thousand in Saskatchewan and thirteen thousand on some lines in Alberta. And when it is recalled that the interest rate was low, that money 
was cheap, and that they did not earn that much money, it becomes of considerable importance that we regard this not as an isolated transaction but in relation to the whole problem; for I am firmly of the opinion that terminals must be provided in Montreal. It is discreditable to the Dominion that the great system of railways which it owns should not have better terminals than it has now in Montreal; they are hardly worthy of the name terminals at Montreal.
They are not, in fact.

No. I have frequently urged on the powers that be the necessity of providing something better in this regard, but I must say that never in the wildest flights of imagination did I contemplate a sum of money so vast as that provided in this bill; nor did I think it possible that we should ever reach the stage where parliament would be willing to commit itself to so vast an expenditure without at least a few more safeguards. It was with these considerations in mind that I desired to look into the situation more fully than I have done. I am speaking, again, from memory-and my memory may not serve me correctly, because as one gets older ones memory does not^-but I recall distinctly the circumstances in connection with that first terminal (bill, and the expenditures made under it, and I think it might assist me in arriving at conclusions, if the minister has other reports of the engineers, to be able to read those reports during the evening. In the meantime, we could go on with other sections of the bill. If the facts are as I think, I have a suggestion to make with regard to an amendment which might be made to this bill.
In connection with the tunnel?

No, in connection with the expenditure. That is predicated entirely upon my being able to satisfy myself about certain facts, because anxious as I am that there should be a terminal at Montreal that will adequately meet every demand which may be made by traffic both for the present and for the future as far as we can reasonably foresee, I am still more anxious that we should not bring about a condition such as followed the vast expenditures of what were really public moneys in this country, the guaranteed securities under the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk Pacific railway schemes. If the minister has not these reports I may be able

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
to obtain them from other sources, although I have not sought to do so, in order to ascertain just what has been said about these terminals.

Let me say at once that in a matter of such importance and such magnitude as that dealt with iby the present bill, I certainly do not want to rash matters and I will undertake to leave the bill in committee until such information as may be desired by any member can be secured. As my hon. friend has said, the proceedings before the railway committee, while they provided a wealth of material, could only deal with specific questions arising in the minds of individuals, if those questions were asked. I am only sorry that he did not avail himself of the privilege which was accorded several other members of this house, who were not members of the committee, but who did ask several questions.
The room was crowded; delegations were present from Montreal, and I did not desire to do so.

I can quite understand that attitude. Now, with regard to the magnitude of this proposal, we must bear in mind the present situation in Montreal as far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned. I think it can be said that we are starting to deal with the problem in Montreal from a much more difficult standpoint than existed in Toronto; we are under very considerably greater handicaps in trying to develop adequate terminal facilities in Montreal than was the case when the start was made in Toronto, and I think hon. members from Toronto will agree that to say the least the situation there was bad enough. In that connection I might point out that the total estimated aggregate expenditure at Toronto by all parties, is $33,000,000; thait is the complete- layout, 'inlcluding the expenditure by all companies, but that only deals with the waterfront and does not include the expenditure by the railway companies individually cut-side thait area. These terminal schemes do cost a lot of money.
Of course, that expenditure was largely occasioned by the separation of grades.
That is also the case in this connection.
But not to the same extent.

If my memory serves me, we are eliminating over 100 grade crossings by this terminal scheme in- Montreal. However, be that as it may, it must be remembered that in Montreal we now have three separate passenger terminals and three separate freight yards, and you cannot get from one to the other by rail except by going around about one hundred miles. The importance of improvement immediately strikes one when these facts are brought out.
Is not that statement just a little strong, with regard to the three separate terminals?
Out to JoLiette.
You said you must travel over one hundred miles to get from one station to another.

In order to deliver anything from the Moreau street station to the Turcotte station or the Bonaventure station requires a journey of over one hundred miles at present; that is, out to Joliette. That is the instance I had in mind. It would be a little shorter to get to the tunnel station, but of course at present there is no freight yard at the tunnel.
With respect to the matter of grade separation west of Bonaventure station, apparently my hon. friend was under the impression that if provision were not made for an inner and outer belt line, that grade separation might not be needed. In that regard I want to assure him that of all the alternative plans which have been developed, none has been brought forward which does not involve the continuous use of the Bonaventure terminal as a freight terminal, and for many years past the great burden of the complaint in Montreal has been the number of grade crossings west of Bonaventure. Grade separation being necessary in any event to accommodate the freight terminal, as I understand it, the suggestion was -made that we might use one or two of the tracks coming in over the separated grade in order to develop suburban inner and outer circles which would serve the large outlying suburban sections of Montreal. Comparatively little extra expense would be involved; the utilization of the existing tracks coming into the freight yards is all th-at is necessary to accomplish it and give a connection from Bonaventure to the tunnel station. As I understand Mr. Palmer's report, he did not recommend that connection; I am relying on memory at the moment in making that statement, but he did recommend an inner and outer belt line system nearer the river than via Bonaventure. That is to say, under Mr. Palmer's scheme as I recall it, the inner belt suburban line would follow up the
2S28

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
harbour tracks from the tunnel station to the harbour, then turn west through the yards and up on the south side of the Bonaventure tracks, joining them in the neighbourhood of St. R'enri.
A very large expenditure was intended to connect the tunnel station with the harbour and with Bonaventure.

Yes, and in that connection I might point out that the original tunnel scheme of the Canadian Northern contemplated such connection from the tunnel station to the harbour tracks; in fact the Canadian Northern did acquire quite a bit of property for right of way down there, which the Canadian National inherited.
Now, with respect to the obligations of the country in regard to the tunnel station, I will gladly get for my hon. friend such information as we have with regard to the present standing of that obligation, but I am sure that any existing obligation is now a part of the general Canadian National obligation in that connection.

This is covered by a
special statute. I could send out and get it, but since the meeting of the committee I have not had an opportunity to do so. My hon. friend will remember that we passed a statute validating an agreement made between the tunnel company of the Canadian Northern and the railway by which, if my memory serves me right, the rental to be paid by the Canadian Northern represented the interest on the terminal securities plus provision for a sinking fund. I thought perhaps the minister would have the information before him, but I can send for it.

I am sorry I have not
it here, but I will be glad to get it and see what bearing it has on the situation, if any.

It means a fixed charge
on terminal facilities.

In any case that still
exists and is part of t'he Canadian National obligation, and whatever we do in Montreal I am afraid it would not affect the monetary situation with respect to that obligation. However, I will be glad to look into that matter and leave the bill in committee in order that we may have an opportunity to examine all phases of the question.
With regard to the engineering inquiry which has been going on for years, I can only say that certainly the government has not pressed this matter unduly. The position of the minister throughout my experience, and I believe former ministers had the same 
view, has been that, with regard to a project of this magnitude, every possible investigation should be made before deciding on a course of action. It is only because the situation has now reached the stage of acuteness which, to my mind, forbids any further postponement, that the government determined to bring the matter forward this year. In connection with great engineering enterprises the minister is naturally a layman and must rely upon a commonsense examination by himself and his officers of the reports of the experts and engineers who have made years of study of the problem involved.
How about the policy?

The minister and the
government must take the responsibility, and do take the responsibility with regard to policy. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was not making any complaint about the policy; he was questioning rather whether we could not at this time solve the problem with a smaller expenditure.
That is right.
In the matter of policy, I think he will agree with me that the Canadian National system must have adequate terminal facilities in the city of Montreal.
I agree with that view.

The Canadian National
has not only inadequate terminals in Montreal at the present time, but they are well-night impossible from the point of view of the handling of traffic. During my personal study of this matter one thing struck me with much force in connection with the experience of great cities in their dealing with terminal problems; I found that that in no single case had the plan been sufficiently broad and sufficiently large. It developed time after time in American cities that the most generous plan, apparently extravagant plan, proved to be inadequate by the time it was carried out, due to the growth of traffic in great terminals. Within the last few months I was told by an officer of the Pennsylvania Railroad Company that the new Pennsylvania terminal in the city of New York, upon which over $100,000,000 was expended, was too small the day it was finished and that further expenditures had to be made because of factors which could not possibly be taken into account at the time the terminal was devised. It has been found necessary to make changes in connection with

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
the Toronto terminal, but in that connection there would be the factor of the lengthened number of years which have intervened since the work was commenced.
There was dead interest for nearly ten years.

But in addition to that, a greater expenditure has been found necessary than was originally contemplated would have to be made. Montreal is not only a great city to-day, but it is apparently destined to be very much greater than it is at the present time.

Ten per cent of all the
people of Canada live on the island.

There is a very large
population there. I will say quite frankly that I have been looking for criticisms based upon the inadequacy of this scheme and a criticism based upon the engineers' failure to envisage a Montreal sufficiently large. With regard to the reports made to the other railway company, I am not in position to speak. The Canadian Pacific management have supplied me with copies of the reports submitted to them. This was a matter of courtesy and I appreciate it very much and the study of those plans has been very useful to me. I will be very glad to let my hon. friend see what I have in that connection.
I will be greatly obliged.

It will be understood that just as the Canadian National approached this matter from the point of view of the interests of the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific approaches it from the point of view of the best interests of the Canadian Pacific.

I approached the matter
from the standpoint of one who has to do with both, and whether or not there could be a joint terminal. Toronto has a joint terminal which provides for the old Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern, the Canadian Pacific and the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo railways.

The hon. member will
appreciate that there is nothing in the scheme now being propounded by the Canadian National which would prevent it being used for a union terminal should the parties agree upon that scheme at any time in the future. I do not think I will be giving away any secrets when I say that the Canadian Pacific very naturally think that the Windsor street station would provide more suitable union terminal facilities than the tunnel station of the Canadian National; the Canadian National believe that the tunnel station would
make a more suitable union station than the Windsor street station. I cannot pretend that there is any agreement between the two companies on that point, but the railway companies are agreeing with respect to other points having to do with the broader matter of terminal" facilities such as economies and joint facilities at various places in and around the city of Montreal; a degree of cooperation which I am satisfied will increase as time passes. There still remains that broad difference between them; both are agreeable to union station facilities but both believe that the best facilities are provided by the stations which they own at the present time. The Canadian Pacific would be quite willing to negotiate for union terminal facilties at the Windsor street station.
How much money would that take?

The Canadian National
would 'be willing to negotiate for union terminal facilities at the tunnel station; each railway company is convinced that the scheme which they suggest would make for the best interests of their particular railway system.
If the Canadian Pacific view were adopted what would be the saving in expenditure?

That question did not
arise because the Canadian National were able to demonstrate to me that such a terminal would not be adequate or satisfactory for their purposes.

The Canadian Pacific
would have such a scheme in contemplation before they would make a suggestion of that character?

I am not aware that
any concrete suggestion was made.
You say that they hold that view.

It was rather a matter
of conference between the parties at my request in order that it might be determined whether or not the best interests of the city of Montreal and the best interests of both railway systems would be better served by a union terminal. There has been a good deal of argument as to whether of not union terminal facilities would be better for the city of Montreal, and I have no doubt that both railway companies went thoroughly into the matter, but, as I say, neither one is agreed as to the economic practicability from their point of view of going into the other's union terminal.

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal

In view of the statement made by the Minister of Railways, should not the government obtain the assistance of competent authorities in order that that question may be decided before such a huge expenditure is made?

Because of the great importance of the issues involved, the government made arrangements to secure the services of Mr. Palmer. The government wanted the problem to be considered in an unbiased way, taking into account the viewpoints of both railway companies and the viewpoint of the people to be served. Mr. Palmer's report has been published and every member of the house has been supplied with a copy. I would point out to the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) that if the government were of the opinion that the tunnel station should be used as a union terminal by both railways, there is no power by which the minister or the government could enforce that view with respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I am very doubtful whether it would be wise to place such power in the hands of any minister or any government. The Canadian Pacific is spending its shareholders' money and must be allowed a reasonable latitude to decide for itself what is best in connection with a matter of that kind.
As to the other point, why should we not compel the Canadian National to go into the Canadian Pacific terminal-
I did not ask that.
No, but I am looking at the question from both sides. My hon. friend asked why the minister did not insist upon a union terminal.

No; I asked why the
government did not investigate the matter on behalf of the people of Canada.

My reply to that is that the government did investigate. There is no doubt parliament could, if it so desired, force the Canadian National into the Canadian Pacific terminal or into a Canadian Pacific union terminal, but in that regard I doubt very much the wisdom of the government or of parliament overriding the unanimous opinion or judgment, based upon years of study, of the responsible officers of the Canadian National railway system. In other words,
I take, in a matter of this kind, the same view of the position of one railway as I do of that of the other. It is very difficult for those of us who are not technical railroad experts to do other than to ensure that the

fullest and most independent inquiry possible has been made and then to take the advice of the responsible officers of the railway system in regard to the solution of the problem.

Did I understand the
minister to say that he had outside opinion and advice in regard to the Canadian Pacific matter?
Yes, Mr. Palmer's report which has been printed and distributed amongst the members.

Mr. Palmer's report is
the one to which the minister refers?

Yes. As to the other
reports secured by the Canadian Pacific, I am quite sure if I do not have them, I can get them.

Mr. Palmer's report is
the only one the government secured?
Yes, from outside sources.
That is what I mean.

I may say that the business of securing reports from outside authorities is rather difficult when we have in Canada just two great railway corporations. It is hard to get within Canada eminent opinion which is not associated with one or other of the two great systems.
It cannot be done.

It is also difficult to
secure that advice from the United States for reasons that will occur to my hon. friend.

It occurred to me, while I was listening to the minister, that it is possible to get expert opinion from the United States. I recall the following terminals: the St. Louis terminal, the Washington terminal. There are certainly three great railway terminals in Chicago, and there is the St. Paul terminal through which every train that goes in or out of St. Paul passes. I think there is a train in and out of that terminal every four minutes of every day in the year.
There is a new terminal in Cleveland.

And a new one in Buffalo.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

I wonder if the minister
would give some explanation of section 2 and its relation to section 7, for the two

sections are very closely related, having in mind at the moment simply the power of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Section 7, to which I must go to interpret what I am going to say in regard to section 2, provides for two powers that shall exercise the right of approval of plans. It reads:
The general plan or plans of the said works and amendments or additions to such general plan at any time made, shall, on the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and Canals, be subject to the approval of the governor in council.
Then- next:
Detail plans affecting any canal or other property controlled by the Department of Railways and Canals shall be subject to the approval of the Minister of Railways and Canals.
Then come these words:
Detail plans of crossings of railways and crossings by the railway of streets or highways shall be subject to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
And lastly:
Detail plans affecting the property of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal shall be subject to the approval of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
I am for the moment concerned only as to the power of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I have not under my band the section of the Railway Act, but the minister may be able to direct me to it. I understand that under the general act the board now has power not only with regard to approving plans of crossings of railway on streets and other railways, but has .power also over station locations. That is exempted 'by the phraseology of this bill. For instance, in section 2 we are giving power to construct terminal stations, local stations, station grounds, yards, and so forth, and all these plans are subject to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners, including highway crossings. I would ask, in the second place, if it is clear in this bill, and if so where, that the Board of Railway Commissioners have the power to pass upon a division of cost where the question of grade construction arises.

First let me send to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition the report made to the Canadian Pacific Railway by C. E. Smith and Company, consulting engineers, St. Louis. It is a report on level crossings construction and railway passenger terminals in the city of Montreal, made in the month of March, 1928. My hon. friend also spoke of some other report.

I was only speaking of
what I saw in the paper.
C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
I believe there is another report, and we will look that up if my hon. friend desires it. ,	.
I understand that the report of the Canadian Pacific Railway was submitted and filed with the Board of Railway Commissioners. Is this the particular report so submitted?

I cannot say whether
this particular report was submitted to the board. I cannot think of any reason why it should be, but it is available.
With reference to the questions raised by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, they really relate to section 7 rather than to section 2, as he indicated. We must bear in mind in considering bills of this character that we are acting in two capacities. We are acting as the shareholders of an enterprise, authorizing capital expenditure by that enterprise.
Who are the shareholders?
We represent them.
I think we represent a very large body of electors, but not necessarily are we the representatives of the shareholders.

Perhaps I can only
answer my hon. friend's interjection in a negative way. If we do not represent the shareholders, they have no representation. We are the only body under the law which can occupy the position of the shareholders of an ordinary company in relation to this particular company. We are the only body which can authorize capital expenditures which in the case of an ordinary company would be authorized by the shareholders.
That is better.

We are acting in that
capacity, and of course we not only have responsibility for this enterprise but must consider also the general transportation interests of the Dominion in enacting legislation.
Section 7 in no particular departs from the practice with respect to the Canadian National enterprise generally in so far as control by the Board of Railway Commissioners is concerned. Under the general legislation creating the Canadian National Railways, the company at the present time does not go to the board for approval of their route maps, but it goes instead to the Minister of Railways. That has been the position since the company was created and is a part of its fundamental legislation.

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal

Except in so far as the
location of stations is concerned.

* There is no exception even in that regard. In that connection may I point out that the place where the Canadian National purposes putting a station in Montreal is already the site of a railway station? They are not proposing to build a station where none now exists, but a larger station on the site of an existing station. For that reason it was not deemed necessary to set out that the Board of Railway Commissioners should pass on the station location. The whole matter was given very considerable thought both by the legal staff of the Canadian National and by the departmental legal Staff, and the reason for section 7 being in its present form is, first, to safeguard this institution, parliament, as representing the shareholders in the matter of controlling the management in the expenditure of a large sum of money; second, to have the same provision with respect to the crossing of canals as would exist in connection with any similar legislation affecting any other railway; third, the same provision respecting the powers of the Board of Railway Commissioners as exists with respect to any other Canadian National enterprise; and fourth, to deal with the harbour commissioners in the only way in which the harbour commissioners can be dealt with so far as ministerial approval is concerned. That is the only answer I think I can give.

I am afraid I shall have to differ a little with the Minister of Railways. As far as I can see it, this section 7 introduces something entirely new in regard to one of the matters covered by it, and that is in regard to the separation of grades, the crossing under or over a highway or a railway. True it is that in 1919 when the act was passed it contained a provision, section 23, which exempted, in effect, the Canadian National Railways from the provisions in regard to the location of stations, for instance. That section says:
With the approval of the governor in council and upon any location sanctioned by the Minister of Railways and Canals, the company may from time to time construct and operate railway lines, branches and extensions, or railway facilities or properties of any description

So that probably the minister is justified in the statement that so far as location of structure or facilities, such as a station, is concerned, the Board of Railway Commissioners may be said to have been left out to some extent.

I do not know the reason for putting it in; possibly it was because the Canadian National Railways was a publicly owned enterprise, but the section was put in the act. Section 13 says:
All the provisions of the Railway Act (excepting those provisions which are inconsistent with this act, and excepting -also the provisions of the Railway Act relating to the location of lines of railway-
That is the only exception.

That is the point to which the minister was referring, that you were not, as a privately owned railway, required to submit ycrnr location, or right of way, plan. The right was given to the governor in council to determine or approve the location but that does not apply to railway and highway crossing plans.
Quite right.

The governor in council may not approve under the act. The practice of the railway board is to hear the application and distribute the costs in regard to separation of grades, amongst the parties interested or affected. It may be a municipality or a street railway. That provision, Mr. Chairman, still applies to the Canadian National Railways. Under this section 7 no question of location of subway, or of under crossing or over crossing, or of the distribution of costs of such works is referred to the Board of Railway Commissioners; it is only the detailed plans of the crossing that shall be subject to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I think the bill goes too far in that respect. I think it may be very soundly argued that when you come to a highway crossing determined upon by the railway, or by the railway in conjunction with the municipality, the Board of Railway Commissioners are concerned not with who shall bear the cost of it -but simply and solely with the detailed plan. I think that is a change in the practice which should be considered very carefully. To begin with, as I understood and read the plans, and noted the models in the railway committee room they provide for certain level crossings and certain streets to be closed, and that without, nominally at all events, the approval or consent of the city of Montreal; it may -be that the parties have got together and have said those are the ones we shall apply for. It seems to me that questions respecting the closing of streets and the diversion of traffic come solely within the powers of the Board of Railway Commissioners and that any plan touching the separation of grades that we approve here

Most hon. members of this house know that I have been urging for a survey of a *coast outlet, not because I expected to get that outlet immediately, but 'because the people want to know just where the branch lines will be built in the Peace River in order to fit in with the outlet when it is ultimately constructed. We have got somewhere in connection with the survey of a possible location of railway branch lines. This I believe to be primarily the responsibility of the federal government. Undoubtedly the control of the location and the construction of railways will be in the hands of the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific and the federal government. Some years ago we were building railways in Canada ahead of the settlers. In some cases we made mistakes in connection with the location of the railways ; in other cases we had duplications, and in other cases we permitted the settlers to go on lands which should never have been settled at all. To-day we are asking the settlers to go out and prove the country before we go ahead with railway construction; we are erring in the other direction. If we adopt the policy of bringing immigrants to this country and expecting them to go out and settle in the newer districts, we have a bounden duty as the federal parliament to see that the settlers obtain railway transportation just as quickly as possible. The same would apply to our own people who are asked to settle on these lands.
I have some criticism to make of the heads of our two railway systems who have been shouting for immigration. I think there will be time enough to shout for immigration when they have provided the last permanent settlement in western Canada with a reasonable amount of railway service, and they have not done that as yet. Settlement in this country is three or four hundred miles ahead of railway development, specially in the Peace River district. I am not blaming the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific for that, because they have just recently taken over the Peace River railway from the Alberta government. The immediate problem to be solved is to provide railway transportation for the five thousand settlers who took up land there last year, and another possible five thousand who will go in this year. In a new country it is absolutely impossible to do anything with regard to the permanent location of schools, hospitals, and so on, until you have the railway into the country or until you know exactly where it is going to be. We cannot avoid hardships and difficulties, but by a wise policy of rail-

Immigration Policy-Mr. Kennedy 


way development we can bring that suffering down to a minimum. In the Peace River block we have an intensely settled district, but it cannot be fully settled until it is supplied with railway facilities. That district is intensely settled sixty miles from a railway, and it justifies the extension of the railway.
As I said a little while ago, I had some difficulty in understanding the proposal offered by the hon. member for North Vancouver. At page 2730 of Hansard, he says:
As to the percentage of the 100,000,000 acres available for agriculture, probably 10 per cent should be allowed for land covered by water. In many districts there is no waste at all. A conservative estimate is 75,000,000 acres of good agricultural land!
Then at page 2731 he makes this statement:
Besides, the best of our districts awaiting settlement to-day are more or less covered with timber of varying density, from open park-life country, light brush or scrub, to the so-called timber land, little of it giving promise of ever becoming of commercial value so far as the timber is concerned. Peace River district is very fortunate. About 50 per cent of that country is what is termed park-like land, and of this at least half is open prairie. Our problem is to make this land available for settlers with the least cost at the earliest possible date.
I do not know whether there are 75,000,000 acres of good land in the Peace River district, but putting these two statements together, it would appear that the hon. member claims that there are 75,000,000 acres of good agricultural land, fifty per cent of which is prairie and park-like land. Prairie land is open land practically ready for the plough and requires no drainage. Then the hon. member states that the other fifty per cent is park-like land. According to these two paragraphs it would appear as though we had 36,000,000 acres of that sort of land in the Peace River district. There have been only about 4,000,000 acres alienated altogether, according to the report which I received from the Department of the Interior. In the Grande Prairie district we have 517,600 acres homesteaded, and we have 1,203,360 acres in the Peace River district.
I would like to read what the hon. member had to say with regard to the question of financing new settlers. At page 2733 of Hansard he says:
It would not require any great administrative ability to assemble and equip clearing units, which might be located at several points, in number sufficient to clear and make available along the lines I have indicated homes for at least 2,000 new settlers a year.
At page 2735 he says:
I proposed last year that the government issue land bonds against their expenditure on such a development. I gave as the maximum required $300,000,000 for a ten year programme, an average of $30,000,000 per year.
Again on the same page he says:
When the settlement of a district is complete, a land value of $30 an acre would be in keeping with the present Peace River values. This means that the homesteader who gets a partially improved homestead for the amount spent on it by the government (which I estimated last year not to exceed $1,500) would not be long in seeing that at $30 per acre for his 160 acre homestead he would have a prospective value of $4,800,
Two thousand homesteads per year at $1,500 each amounts to $3,000,000, but the program suggested amounts to $30,000,000, which would mean 20,000 homesteads per year. I am a little confused when I consider those figures. The hon. member seems to have dropped or added a cipher in one of these statements.
I am in accord with his suggestion that transportation is absolutely essential and must be brought close to the settlers, and that we should develop some scheme of financing the settler. In 1926 two bills were presented to the house which, although not along the line of the proposition recommended by the hon. member for North Vancouver, had that very matter in view.
I am also in sympathy with the proposition of clearing the land by fire. I agree with the bon. member's statement that a large percentage of the park-like land could be handled for about $12 per acre. I speak from experience in connection with that because I had some cleared and turned over last year which cost me just about that much; yet I do not see whjr we should go ahead with a scheme involving an expenditure of $6 per acre for clearing when we can handle it by fire for less than $1 per acre.
The amendment directs the whole criticism at the Minister of Immigration, and to me that seems to be striking the wrong head. We should criticize three or four departments if we come to the conclusion that it is necessary to accept a scheme of that kind in order to have a government which is right up to the standard of what Canada needs. It would require the cooperation of the Railway department, and the railways as well, both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National; it would require the cooperation of the Department of the Interior, the department which demonstrated conclusively in 1919 that land could be cleared cheaply by fire but which has not gone ahead with a development in that way. It would require the cooperation of the Department of Immigration as well.
I am heartily in accord with the Minister of Immigration when he takes the stand that immigration brought into this country must be controlled in relation to the needs of labour and the conditions prevailing in the country and that we should not bring in any imnr

grants whom we cannot place or for whom we cannot find work. I do not believe that it is feasible to bring in a large number of new immigrants and place them away out on the frontier in a block by themselves. The immigrant should come here and obtain his experience by working for some other farmer for two, three or five years. Then he would be in a position to go and select his land or buy his farm. By that time he would have formed1 a pretty good idea of the kind of farm he wanted and the price he could pay for it. If you put a block of green Scotchmen, Englishmen or any other class away out on the prairies by themselves, especially in a year when there is a crop failure, you have not in your settlement the element that can take the long view and steady the settlement through to the good years which are sure to come. In the new settlements what you want are people of experience in doing the kinds of farming necessary in a new district, or a very liberal mixture of them in order to guide and steady the newcomers. For that reason, while I have not been altogether satisfied with everything the government has done and while I am also not prepared to condemn the scheme advanced by the hon. member for North Vancouver, because there are a number of good ideas in his speech, I feel that his amendment does not fit in with the constructive ideas in his speech, and therefore I cannot support the amendment.

I should
like to make a few remarks in regard to the immigration policy of this government. We have been spending in the neighbourhood' of five to six million dollars a year in order to secure immigrants whom we consider are necessary. It does not appear from the general criticism which has been directed toward the government and its immigration policy that that money has been as well spent as it should have been, or that we are getting the service that we should be getting for our expenditure on immigration in general. I take it that we are all agreed that if the Immigration department were functioning with full efficiency we would' be getting better results. I am going to quote from the report of the Department of Immigration for the year ending March 31, 1928, in order to show that some of the remarks of the minister and his department hardly fit in. For instance, at page 59 I find the following remark from the commissioner in regard to the publicity work in his department. It is headed "Films":
Films-There is an increasing demand for the use of films, and during the year the supply at the London office was frequently insufficient

A booklet to which very wide distribution is given is called "Canada West". As its name suggests, it deals with the western provinces of Canada-Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia. This booklet is printed in three editions: one designed for distribution in Great Britain, one for the United States, and one printed in French, used mainly for repatriation purposes in French-speaking communities in the New England states. That shows beyond any question of doubt-and it is reflected throughout the whole of the criticism of the Immigration department-that within the department itself there is a certain amount of disorganization which could easily be remedied by efficient cooperation. As regards the question that is immediately before us, the amendment moved by the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae),
I was rather surprised and startled to hear the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) say that he could not agree with the scheme outlined by the hon. member for North Vancouver. But after listening to what he had to say on the matter, I came to the

Immigration Policy-Mr. Fraser
conclusion that he was not very far from agreeing with the hon. member for North Vancouver. His argument to prove that it is not exactly the scheme we must have seemed to me to prove that it was a pretty efficient scheme and its adoption provided that the details were worked out by men with the proper spirit for the task, would result in much greater efficiency in the Department of Immigration than we have at the present time.
After listening to the information which has been given to the house during the last three or four sessions in regard to the Peace River country, one cannot doubt that we have in that section of Canada a very large area- whether it is 75,000,000 or 50,000,000 acres does not alter the question very much-which is capable of vast development. The Canadian people by their characteristics are well qualified for the task of bringing that large area under settlement, and, given proper direction, of making it productive. What we require is an administration which as a whole has caught the vision of that northern country and its possibilities, and which will lay down policies and courageously follow them out in order that the development of that country may proceed with some degree of rapidity.
It has been stated time and again in the house that the proper way to develop that northen country is to give it an outlet to the Pacific coast, and until that outlet is given the Peace River country cannot develop as it properly should. The reason is plain to any person who will take into consideration the location of the district. The whole land is situated not more than 800 or 900 miles from the Pacific coast, whereas there is a haul of 3,000 miles at the very least in order to bring the produce to the eastern seaboard. Therefore we do not need any argument to prove that it is necessary to connect that district by the shortest line possible with the Pacific coast. It is in that respect, and in that alone, that I find most fault with the present Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) and the present government. The hon. member for Peace River did not like to unload the whole responsibility on the Minister of Immigration, and perhaps I should not attempt to unload on him the lack of railway facilities in that section, but at the same time, had we in the position of Minister of Immigration a man who had caught the vision of that section, who was seized of its possibilities and who had made up his mind to develop it, I feel certain that the railway development there would have progressed further than it has so far. To that extent I must hold the Minister
of Immigration responsible for lack of railway development in the Peace River country. As a matter of fact, the western prairies have been settled and brought to their present stage of production because behind the organization of effort in that territory there were men who had caught the vision, who were seized of the possibilities and who were determined to give the country the opportunity to develop. At the present time I believe that the responsible officials of the government are not properly seized of the possibilities in that country, that they have not caught the vision, and are not evolving and following out progressive policies which would reflect credit on the Canadian people in the development of an empire such as we have in that part of the country.

At six o'clock I think I
had shown to the satisfaction of every reasonable person that the Department of Immigration and Colonization was not achieving the results that it should. It may be well to review for a few minutes some of the statements that have been made by the present government through its ministers and by officials connected therewith, having to do with the matter now under consideration. ^
In the first place, I would like to remind the house of the promises made by the present Prime Minister during the election campaign of 1925. I think it will be recalled by most hon. members that during his campaign in western Canada, referring to the immigration policy of the government which he hoped then to lead, he made or is reported to have made the statement that the spearhead of his immigration policy would be directed towards the Peace River country. Well, since then we have had four or five years of government under his leadership, and what has been the result? What has happened to that spearhead? It seems to me that it is very badly blunted and bent. It looks to me as if the platform then laid down was pretty much the same as that on whioh he was supposed to attain office in 1919. If that was not so, certain it is that the policy which has been directed towards the colonization of the northern country has not been a very energetic one, and the results achieved have been feeble and futile.
Strong men and women have gone to that country to help in its development, they have pointed out the possibilities of that country

Immigration Policy-Mr. Fraser
if proper opportunities are afforded for its development. Yet the present government has not supplemented as it should the efforts of those early pioneers, nor does it look as though they may expect to get much assistance from the present administration.
Then we have the president of the Canadian National Railways, who, when he visited the Peace River country in 1925 to inspect it at first hand and examine into its possibilities made the statement that if the people in that district would produce 10,000,000 budhels of grain he would be prepared to give consideration to their railway problems. The people of the Peace River country took him at his word. They went diligently to work, and in the year 1927 they not only raised 10,000,000 bushels of grain but actually shipped out over the railways 11,000,000 bushels, thus carrying out their part of the bargain in full measure. And what has the president of the Canadian National Railways since that time done to carry out his part of the bargain? When he was asked the other day in the railway committee what the'situation was in regard to the implementing of that promise he said "Well, just the same answer as you get from this government when you ask them on any vital question-it is still under consideration." In 1925 the promise was made. The people accepted it in good faith. They did their part, and now in 1929, four years later, the answer of the president of the Canadian National Railways is that the matter is "still under consideration."
The Minister of Immigration says we are doing very well so far as immigration is concerned. Perhaps we are. The members of the cabinet draw very comfortable salaries. They spend about half a million dollars on motor cars and gasoline in travelling around the country looking after official business-
That is terrible.
Awful.
Some was spent in Europe.

-while the farmers in the Peace River country producing their crops are despoiled of $6,500,000 for lack of railway facilities which should be provided by this government. I arrive at that conclusion in this way: the Peace River country in 1927 produced 11,000,000 bushels of grain. I presume they produced as much in 1928. It cost the .people in the Peace River block 30 cents per bushel to haul that grain to railhead; if you multiply the 30 cents by the 22,000,000 bushels, you will find it amounts to about $6,500,000. In view of that condition, it is not astonishing that we should ask what is the horizon of the Minister

of Immigration. Is he giving consideration to those areas which are a considerable distance from his own little corner of Manitoba called Pipestone? If he is thinking only, of his own little district of Pipestone then he is merely indulging in a kind of pipe dream.
The Prime Minister's spearhead is bent and blunt. The Minister of Immigration sobs, with drooping head, "It is well enough", and the president of the Canadian National Railways says he is "giving consideration" to the cry of the people. Surely it is time the development of such areas should be placed in stronger hands, under the direction of people who have a clear vision of the possibilities of that great country and an appreciation of what we expect of them in relation to the development of this country.
But there is another angle to this immigration policy to which I wish for a few minutes to direct the minister's attention. What has the Department of Immigration and Colonization done towards the colonizing of their own lands in the .province of British Columbia? They have in that province, in the Peace River block and along the railway belt, large areas of very good land. Will the Minister of Immigration tell me what well organized, well directed effort they have ever made to colonize those areas, outside of the colonization effort under the Soldier Settlement Board; whether they have ever made any effort, whether they have had a colonization agent in any .part of those areas? Not only that, but they have very important interests also in British Columbia so far as the Grand Trunk Pacific is concerned. Along that line of railway they have never made any effort to help colonization. All along that line there is good land, there are industrious people, an excellent climate, and as good soil as you can find anywhere in the world; yet this country is not as prosperous as it should be, and a line built to the highest standard of any railway in the Dominion of Canada, with the best possible grades, is being operated as a second class branch line. During the summer they operate a railway service six days in the week, but they provide the business people along that line with a mail service only three days weekly. That does not assist in the colonization of an area of that kind. The minister says that he is willing to cooperate with any of the provincial governments in assisting immigration, but I say he has made no effort to colonize that part of the country with which I am acquainted.

Will the hon. member tell
the house what advantages he hopes to gain for Canada by the immediate settlement of this last virgin' district we have left?

I suppose it will have to
remain unsettled so long as this government is in power and so long as the hon. member keeps it in power. I said a moment ago that we had in Canada, if we went about it in the proper way, all the materials for a satisfactory colonization of that great country. Now, someone might ask where the people would come from. Well, the first thing to which I would direct the attention of the minister would be the number of people annually leaving Canada. I submit with all sincerity that if proper efforts were directed to these new districts these 50,000 people would be very glad to remain in Canada and find employment here instead of going across the line to look for work. As a matter of fact the line of our population in Canada requires broadening, and there is no section of the Dominion where the opportunities to broaden this line are as favourable as they are in northern Alberta and northern British Columbia. Mr. Speaker, while I cannot agree with the amendment that has been placed before the house by the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae), I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating him on giving to the house a well thought out scheme of dealing with our very important immigration problem. I think the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Porke) stated during his debate that while he has been the subject of a great deal of criticism from time to time, the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for North

Immigration Policy-Mr. Lucas
Vancouver is the first constructive suggestion that he has received. I am sure the house will agree with me when I say that the hon. member for North Vancouver must have given a great deal of time and thought to this question, and must have gone to a great deal of expense to develop the scheme which he has placed before us.
So far as I am concerned, I must say that I cannot agree with that scheme, first because we are still quite young out in Alberta, and we have hopes that if we live to a reasonable age we will some time in the not too distant future get control of our natural resources.
I am not in favour of delegating to the Dominion government the control of a vast area in the province of Alberta for the purposes of colonization. That is something about which the province should have a great deal to say, especially with regard to the number and class of settlers that they admit. In the second place, I think the member for North Vancouver was wrong in directing his amendment only against the Department of Immigration. If we had to deal only with the amendment it might be very hard to vote against it, but it is the scheme that is outlined in connection with the amendment to which I take objection. The amendment says in part:
This house regrets the failure of the government to profit by Canadian experience in the colonization and settlement of the country and deplores the fact that men and women have, during recent months, been settled on western Crown lands at great distances from transportation, educational, hospital and other facilities, thereby making it almost impossible for them to achieve success and happiness in their new surroundings.
With that part of the amendment I think every hon. member will heartily agree, and if that policy had been adopted in the early settlement of the country I am sure we would have met with a great deal more success. It is too late now to go back to the older settled portions of the country in order to apply some of the ideas which the hon. member for North Vancouver has laid before the house. However, some of them might be adopted yet, by applying block settlement in the undeveloped sections of our country. I do not believe it is fair to the new settler to allow him to go at random hundreds of miles from the railway and then leave him stranded there, because if that is done he will not be able to make a success.
Coming now to the latter part of the amendment:
-and is of the opinion that such conditions can only be remedied by immediate reorganization of the Department of Immigration and Colonization.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the reorganization of the Department of Immigration and Colonization will not remedy the situation. This amendment should have been directed either against the whole government, or against the Department of the Interior, which has the mapping and blocking out of the homesteads. Once those lands are blocked out and put on the market, as it were, for settlers, I take it that the Immigration and Colonization Department is not responsible.
The hon. member for North Vancouver in outlining this scheme, as I understood him, said that in this block settlement a settler would receive a homestead at possibly a valuation of $1,500 for improvements; that with concentration this territory would develop very rapidly, the land would soon reach the value of improved land in older settled districts, and I think he mentioned a sum of approximately $30 an acre. In my opinion Mr. Speaker, if that plan were adopted it would mean an exodus from our older settled districts, because the man who was heavily involved, who had a heavy debt hanging over him, would be certainly well advised to throw up his farm, go into this new district and take up land where he would have an overhead of only $1,500 to start with, in the knowledge that within a very short time, because of this concentrated development, the value of the land would increase to approximately $30 an acre.
If there is any criticism to make in regard; to the government, I would say that they have not attributed to this immigration problem the importance it deserves, because until the present minister was appointed the Department of Immigration and Colonization did not have a minister of its own. It was treated more or less as a subsidiary.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the immigration question in Canada is one of the most important problems that we are faced with to-day. When we consider Canada as a young, practically undeveloped country, covering a vast area, in fact greater in area than that of the United States, with immense natural resources, capable of sustaining a population of almost unlimited numbers and at the present time with only nine or ten million people. If the minister -who has boasted that he is a Scotch settler, and I am sure we are proud of that fact were himself obliged to experience the conditions under which these men are trying to make good, and were loaded down with the burdens that they bear, he would certainly do some spuealing too.
In conclusion I would say that the cases which I have dealt with prove that people are being brought to this country under conditions that are not desirable and not in the best interests of immigration. It is, in other words, mighty poor advertising. These people
