What is the use of bringing in more people to put them in a' condition like that? What we are actually doing through our general policy in Canada is to over-industrialize Canada instead of trying to help agriculture. The manufacturers, transportation people and bankers are the people who get the best break in Canada. Our immigration policy reminds me of a person who is constantly having a hemorrhage of his purest blood and trying to keep his health up by having a blood infusion. It is poor preventive medicine, but that is the kind of thing we are doing in the Dominion of Canada.
Who are the people who want immigrants? The railways want immigrants. The banks want immigrants. The manufacturers want immigrants, and theTe are a few farmers who want cheap labour and think they can get it that way. These people who want immigrants want to bring in more and more of them, and- the greener the immigrant the richer the harvest. I think if your take those groups of people out you would not have anybody who wanted to pour immigrants into this country.
I had the privilege of addressing some sixty gatherings in western Canada last year, and twenty odd in Ontario, and I found that the people were more interested in this subject than any .other. If you could have heard some of the real farmers laugh at the members of parliament over this subject, and at the government-well it was refreshing to my soul.
I want to propose an immigration policy for the Minister of Immigration. I do not want to' be destructive, so I will attempt to be 
constructive. I would not spend one dollar of state money on immigration-not a dollar. I would do nothing to induce people to come to this country. The Minister of Immigration has stated that the most of what he heard was destructive, not constructive. I should like to recall to the mind of the minister this very proposal that was made time without number in our own caucuses and at our own conferences before he saw fit to cross the floor of the house, and had he taken with him the wisdom he found there he would be even a better minister of immigration than he is-and at that he is better than the one we had before. That as the opinion that is held by farmers throughout Canada. They do not want to see money spent on immigration. I remember a speech that was made one time, quite near morning, by the member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I am not sure whether it was in 1922 or 1923, but if the Minister of Immigration wants to read about farm conditions let him get that speech and read it. I have not heard as good a speech on the subject since.
If I were going to spend any money on immigration I would spend every bit of it on inspection, inpecting those who come into Canada, in order to see that we got the very best. And I would not go fishing for those, either, telling them a whole lot of things that have not even a resemblance to the truth. I remember last year the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. WoodSworth) stating that domestics were induced to come to Canada by telling them there were three hundred thousand surplus men in Canada. What a terrible disappointment must have awaited some of the new women! But if we are to have immigrants coming into this country I would have a very rigid examination of them to see that they were physically healthy and that they were mentally sound, We have not had a careful enough or rigid enough inspection of the people that we have let into Canada in the last few years, although I think it has been a little more rigid than it was before. But even yet, if some of the specimens I have seen coming in this year are general, then all the worse for Canada. And so I would be very, very careful about the kind of people that we let in. But as a farmer representative in this house I must again protest about having only farmers and domestics come in. Let all classes come in who want to come if they are physically and mentally fit, and I would not restrict it to any one nation. What we need in this country is a virile people, people who are not

afraid to face the climate we have or afraid to face any condition, and who can adapt themselves to new environment.
The wheat crop of the world for 1928 exceeded the crop of 1923, which was a bumper crop by 300,000,000 bushels. We need not go on thinking that we can continue increasing our output of wheat without affecting the price of wheat, as I think wheat prices are beginning to show. I want to quote very briefly from a speech made by George Mclvor, who is the general sales manager of the Canadian wheat pool. He says:
I do not wish to overemphasize the large production of grains in 1928, as the other side of the picture, namely, the very heavy consumption of wheat this year, is very important, but I do wish to make it perfectly clear that the supply of bread grains relative to the demand for same is considerably larger than last year and, of course, it naturally follows that the supply will be disposed of at lower prices than those prevailing a year ago.
Any sensible person who knows that if you increase and increase your production you will finally decrease or lower your prices. People after all can eat only so much, and while it is true that when the standard of living begins to rise in the oriental countries there will be more bread grains consumed there, it is also true that as the standard of living goes even higher, as it is in this country and some other countries, less bread grains are consumed. The people use other things, and do not consume as much wheat as they did before.
A farmer who lives in my constituency was telling of an amusing experience he had with immigrants, and as a matter of fact this experience was rather coming to him. Last winter we had a long discussion on this subject of immigration. He still thought that it was a very good thing for the man who owned the land to bring in immigrants in order that he might get someone cheap to work for him, and so he proceeded to test out his own theory. He got quite a good looking and really cleveT fellow, an immigrant. He was to stay a year. He came in the fall, stayed until the beginning of seeding and then left. He tried for another, and one came to his town and he went out to get him. It was a cold and blue sort of day. The farmer met the boy, for he was nothing more than that, and brought him to where his team and wagon were and told him he would be back in a moment. When he came back the boy was missing. They instituted a search and located him. When they got near him he took to his heels and fled, and that was the last of him. So he tried a third one, and he told me without any hesitation at all that he
wished heartily this last one would follow the example of his predecessor. That is his experience, and he is now coming round to my position on the immigration problem.
I am not going to quote resolutions passed by farm organizations; the Minister of Immigration is familiar with them. He knows the position of agriculture in the matter, and as this is an immigration policy that affects agriculture, then agriculture should be consulted; they should have the say as to what is to be done. As soon as other classes are willing that their numbers should 'be * added to from other countries then they have the right to say what is to be done, but not until then.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put there are a few things that I desire to say, more particularly as this question of immigration has been one of great interest to the farmers of the west, and especially to the farmers of Alberta. They have taken such a keen interest in this question that they have never failed to notify the department from time to time, through their conventions, as to what their ideas in respect to the matter were, and I am going to take a few minutes before the question is put to emphasize to the minister and to the house one or twto of the points which perhaps have not been brought out by previous speakers as definitely as they might have been.
I note, of course, that the minister is saying that he has had no constructive suggestions. I think he made an exception of the suggestion which came from the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae). But I venture to observe that certain constructive suggestions have come from the United Farmers of the west. They may have been suggestions with which he did not agree, or he may be in a position to-night or some other time to reveal the weaknesses of those suggestions. But that they were constructive there can be no doubt, and I hope if he has overlooked them so far he will take them into his serious consideration in the immediate future. One of these constructive suggestions I can put in a very brief form.
I am not certain just exactly how much is being expended on immigration. I know we are about to vote in this house approximately $7,000,000. Some of this goes to one thing and some to another; I do not know how much goes to immigration and how much to something else. Now the minister assures us to-night, in an aside, that we shall not spend much more than slightly over $1,000,000 directly on immigration. But cer-

Immigration Policy-Mr. Irvine
tain it is that we are going to vote over $3,000,000 having to do with immigration. If only $1,000,000 of this sum is expended in the actual work of immigration and $2,000,000 close by or near to immigration, then the minister, I am sure, will have considerable explaining to do. But I do not think we can go beyond the vote of $3,500,000 in the estimates directly accounted for by immigration expenditures. Now here is a constructive suggestion which I would offer the minister- and it comes direct from the lips of the farmers of the west. Instead of continuing to spend that $3,500,000 in an immigration policy which, for a number of reasons, is absolutely futile, it would be far better political economy and far better for Canada as a nation if that amount were expended in assisting young Canadians who desire to take up agriculture. That, I submit, is a constructive suggestion. The minister may find some reasons why it should not be adopted; he may be able to show us its faults. So far he has not done so; so far as we can see, that $3,500,000 will continue to be spent in bringing to this country people who go out as fast as they come in. The minister has not said to us that he 'has given the suggestion consideration and finds it cannot be seriously entertained. However, I leave it with him as one constructive suggestion and I hope he will give us a reply, either now or during the discussion of his estimates. Before I am through I shall place on Hansard a number of resolutions passed by organizations in my own riding, as well as resolutions passed by larger organized agricultural bodies, to indicate that the question of immigration is one of great importance to them and that they do think they have at least some constructive suggestions to put forward.
May I for a moment digress to say that I am not levelling any criticism at the Department of Immigration; I fancy that department is just as efficiently run as any other. I am criticising the policy of immigration as such and I shall try to show to the minister and the house that that immigration policy does not belong to the immediate present; it is an immigration policy which had its origin in narrow class desire. There was perhaps a time in the history of Canada when that immigration policy was a great deal more serviceable than it is at the present moment, but I shall try to show that, in the light of certain developments which are now taking place in the country, to continue the present policy is utter folly.
The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphai!) emphasized the fact that this immi-

gration policy is a class policy. It is a class policy in its origin. It is actually believed, I understand, fairly sincerely by land speculators, that Canada will become more prosperous if more people come into the country; it is believed by railroad companies that Canada will become more prosperous if more people come in; it is believed by banks and ordinary business concerns that Canada will increase in prosperity with an increase in population. Well, we can understand these people, and perhaps from their narrow point of view it would appear to them that greater prosperity must result from an increase in population. Of course, there will be more railway tickets sold; there will be perhaps a little increase in banking; there will be more potatoes and beef and biscuits and so forth sold if our population increases in number. But looking at the question from the national point of view, it will be seen at once that this is after all a narrow class view to take of it, and those who have advocated that policy and who advocate it to-day have obviously not taken all the factors into consideration. The present immigration policy is furthermore a class policy in its effects. The Canadian policy to-day, as it is applied, is strictly speaking a class policy.
Again, the hon. member for Southeast Grey has gone so far as to point out specifically that we would not object if the Immigration department, should undertake to bring in a large number of lawyers or doctors. We can apply exactly the same argument to doctors which the hon. member for North Vancouver used in reference to the prairies. The hon. member points out, and quite properly, that there are vast areas of land that can be put under cultivation, that there is a great deal of brush that might be cut, that machines could do the cutting, with immigrants to operate those machines. No one will question that; the hon. member's analysis is perfect in this respect. But might I not point out that annually we have great waves of measles, great waves of whooping cough, great waves of flu, providing any amount of work for doctors-far more doctors than we now have in Canada. It would be as wise to advocate that we should increase the number of our doctors by means of immigration because of periodic attacks of flu as it is to say that because we have large stretches of uncultivated land we should have more immigrants. That is not sound reasoning from the economic point of view; it is perfectly logical from any other standpoint, but absolutely meaningless from the economic. I suggest, then, that some consideration must be given Canada's immi-

gration policy strictly from the economic point of view, and before I am through I shall indicate something of my meaning in that regard. It is assumed-for what reason I am at a loss to know-that agriculture can absorb almost any number of people; I believe the hon. member for North Vancouver went so far as to suggest 2,000,000 people more for the Peace River district alone. Why not make it 4,000,000? I do not see why anyone should stop at 2,000,000. If we are siure of placing 2,000,000 may we not stretch a point and make it 4,000,000?
I say it is assumed, apparently without any reason whatever, that agriculture can absorb an indefinite number of immigrants, and it is assumed, I take it, on this basis: that inasmuch as there are a great many millions of acres of land yet untilled, and many hundreds of millions of pigs yet unborn, which farmers could look after, therefore there is work for any number of farmers to do. That is the reasoning. But there cannot be an unlimited number of anything in connection with any industrial enterprise; we cannot have an unlimited number of miners, and unlimited number of carpenters, an unlimited of doctors, notwithstanding what I said a moment ago about the periodic breaking out of diseases which might provide employment, temporarily at any rate, for many more doctors than we have. These professions and classes and industrial groups cannot be increased indefinitely. How, then, is it assumed that agricultural pursuits have no limit? Who is the oracle who insists upon that philosophy? Since when has agriculture been outside the laws of supply and demand any more than carpentry or medicine? Surely no one will seriously entertain that idea. Yet there can be no other basis for such an argument. Well, if it is not true that agriculture is beyond the law of supply and demand, by what reasoning do those who advocate a continued increase in immigration, and particularly in agricultural help and agriculturists generally, come to such a conclusion as I have indicated? Just because there is land not yet cultivated? Just because there are millions of pigs yet unborn? Just because there are some places where scrub still grows? Is that an economic reason why more people should be brought in at public expense? The time has come when there should be a little more clear thinking on this question, and particularly on the part of men who come from western Canada.
Let me come now to what I regard as the important phase of the present situation. No one will deny that agriculture is passing, and

indeed passing swiftly, through a period of development. When that development has been completed we will have an agricultural industry which will not be recognized when compared with what it is to-day. Agriculture is gradually becoming industrialized, and that process is always followed by organization, copitalization and specialization. I do not believe that any advice of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) or any advice out of the profound farming experience of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) will stay the natural evolutionary process of this great industry. Let me give the Minister of Immigration an illustration. I can take him to one of the most beautiful valleys in Canada.
Is that Pipestone?
It is one much more beautiful than Pipestone.
Pipe dream.

And I can show him one hundred farmers who have settled along the river there. On a cold winter's morning those one hundred farmers will get up, early of course, and they start one hundred gasoline engines to pump a few buckets of water to one hundred little groups of pigs-one gasoline engine would drown every pig in the whole valley. The industry is overcapitalized and every individual farmer is impoverished. He is endeavouring to industrialize himself and at the same time to hold on to the conditions of peasantry from which the industry has evolved. I suggest that agriculture is standing at 'the parting of the ways. It must follow the views of the Minister of Agriculture and go back to peasantry by the route of mixed farming, or else it must go forward to organization, centralization and specialization. Which of the two is it going to follow? If we are to go forward to centralization and specialization, as I believe will be the inevitable tendency, then to bring in more farmers will either put a stress upon those whom you bring in as well as uipon those Who are already here, or will drag the whole thing back to . the days of peasantry. It may be all very well to put another one hundred farmers into that valley and have every one of them start with a few cattle and pigs and a gasoline engine; that may be all right for the manufacturers of gasoline engines but it is not good business and it is not following the natural order of events in respect to the industrial development which is taking place before our very eyes. I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that with proper organization, capital-

Immigration Policy-Mr. Irvine
ization and specialization there is a sufficient number of farmers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta properly to farm every foot of land in those three provinces. Instead of trying to fill up these so-called vacant lands with individuals without money and without experience or knowledge either of the country or of agriculture, if the ministers of immigration and agriculture would lend their best intelligence and direct the country's best efforts toward encouraging better organization, sounder finance, closer specialization, greater centralization and increased output with the resultant reduction in overhead, they would be filling a long-felt want of the western agriculturist. The western farmer is in the position to-day which the small business interests were in during the time of keen competition before the great mergers took place and before industrialism was so well established. I think the Minister of Immigration said something; would he kindly say it loudly enough so that I can understand him? If it is not meant for me, of course I do not want to hear it.
The hon. member has been *reading Harper's Magazine.

No, I have not; but if it was anything like what I am saying it was very good. I commend Mr. Harper, or whoever it was wrote the article, on having been able to appreciate the situation. That is ithe situation as I see it with reepectt to agriculture in the west, and I believe that specialization and proper organization has scarcely begun.
Then there is the question of production itself. There is no doubt that if a boot and shoe factory in Canada increased its output there would be great danger of blocking the market unless the purchasing power could be increased to an amount which would equal the increase of production. The same is trud of live stock, of dairy products, of horticultural products and of agricultural products, because none of them are immune from the law of supply and demand. It may be all very well for the railway companies, the banks, or organized business to make a great hip-hurrah about getting more people to come to Canada and go on the farms, but in doing that they are, first, reducing the standard of living of every farmer by increasing the suipply of goods without increasing the demand; and second, the country will be flooded with immigrants, progress will be blocked and we will be back to the old Russian peasantry days. If we follow our present immigration poiicy we will be going towards the days of peasantry, whereas if we follow the other we will be striving for proper organization.

I should like to read to the house a few of the resolutions which have been passed within the last month or so in the riding of Wetaskiwin. The first one, passed by Pleasant Hill Local No. 008 of the United Farmers of Alberta, reads as follows:
Resolved, that whereas, through the years we have all known cases of capable, promising, Canadian young men who wish to follow farming, but for lack of means were compelled to leave the country;
Therefore, in our opinion, while our government is evolving plans to aid British immigrants, we believe it would be wise and fair to include in such plans as much help for Canadian boys and men who desire and possess the qualifications to settle on farms.
The organization authorized the gentleman who signed this resolution, Mr. J. P. Beach, the secretary, to forward the resolution to the Minister of Immigration, and a copy was sent to myself. A similar resolution was passed by the Lacombe Women's Institute, and is signed by Mrs. E. L. Misener, secretary. Practically the same resolution was passed by the Progressive local of the United Farmers of Alberta and was forwarded here. Another resolution was sent through the Lacombe Local. This was passed by the Lakeside Woman's Institute and is signed by Mrs. Arthur Bauer.
I have another resolution which was passed at the annual convention of the United Farmers of Canada. No doubt the minister has received a copy of this, but I do not know whether or not he regards it as a constructive suggestion. I am not going to read it as a constructive suggestion, but rather as indicating that the farmers of Saskatchewan as well as of Alberta, are not satisfied with what might be called the blind immigration policy now being followed in Canada. The resolution reads:
Whereas this convention is opposed to the present method of securing immigrants;
Therefore be it resolved that we urge the federal government to appoint a national commission of inquiry with just representation thereon from organized labour and organized agriculture, that shall study the problem of immigration and assimilation from every possible angle, such commission to conduct public hearings to make provision for the attendance of representative witnesses whose testimony shall be taken under oath, and to report to parliament the conclusion reached by it and make such recommendations as in its judgment it may deem proper, and that pending the findings of such a commission, no further agreement shall be entered into by the federal government with the railroads after the present agreement has expired.
In conjunction with that resolution I would make one final constructive suggestion and offer it for the minister's consideration, namely, that he drop the present immigration

policy entirely. He may regard that as a destructive suggestion, but it would save a considerable amount of money even if nothing were done. As I suggested in my opening remarks, Canada would be better off from an economic point of view. Moreover, we would escape the difficulties which result from assisting immigration out of the taxes paid by the people, whose burden is now as heavy as they can bear without our bringing others here to compete with them in what they are actually producing, thus lowering their standard of living. I hope the minister will give due consideration to the suggestions that have come from this section of the house, and that the immigration policy which is now calling for at least $3,500,000, will be discontinued until such time as the government knows what is the best kind of policy to pursue.

The government of the day announced in its platform of 1919 the best immigration policy that I have ever heard announced, either in this house or out of it, but I am sorry to say that they have never carried it out. This country was hardly settled when there was placed' a load on agriculture to assist every other industry under the sun. That load is there to-day, and agriculture is falling down under it. The Liberal party in 1919 had a platform which, as regards tariff planks, constituted the best immigration policy ever put forward in this country, but they failed to carry it out. If they would to-day scrap the Immigration department and, so to speak, step on the gas in implementing the tariff policy enunciated in that platform, they would do more to stimulate immigration of the agricultural classes than anything else they could undertake. The farmer is up against it tc-day at every turn owing to the assisting of industry in other lines, industries that will permit no competition whatever, that will not have immigration that may affect their industry, but that are willing that the farmer shall have all the competition they can give him. At the same time the farmer must provide assistance for industry to the tune of 20, 25 or 30 per cent. Let us relieve agriculture of some of this burden. Agricultural machinery, it is true, is not taxed to any great extent, perhaps an average of 10 per cent, but many articles that are used on the farm are taxed 25 or 30 per cent and even more. Even the rough clothing that the farmer and his family wear about the farm is taxed from 30 to 35 per cent; yet the government revised the schedules only last session and left them at these ridiculously high levels. If we want to assist agriculture let us relieve it of some of the burdens it now carries for the assistance of all the other industries of this country, and we shall have done something which agriculture can appreciate and from which it will benefit. I hope the government will realize that if they would put into effect their tariff platform of 1919 they could give some relief to the farmer, and it would prove to be one of the best immigration policies that has been presented to this country in years.

The appointment was made
on the recommendation of the deputy minister because of the increased work. At present the staff is overworked. I know that some of them go back after dinner many nights to do their work. The appointment is absolutely necessary.
What has occurred during the last year to increase the work of the department so that an assistant commissioner is needed?

There has been increased
immigration, and if my hon. friend will look through the estimates he will find other services that have brought about an increase of work. New bridges have been opened up, for instance, where immigration work has to be done. It is often overlooked that there is in the Immigration department a preventive service requiring a large number of employees.
That is a work that has to be carried on even if no immigrants come in; we still have to have officers along the border for the purpose of examining those who enter the country for any purpose. There are one or two bridges on the St. Lawrence river where we require officials for that purpose. All this has increased the work of the staff.
